items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: So he said, uh-uh, you can't make it like that. He said, you better learn some music. So he started to show him.

ctx.x: I could just whistle something up and pick the horn up and blow it. I don't know what key I was on unless I knew I played. And, uh, who taught you how to read it? Well, I liked something in the Army. I stole my reading. That's the truth I stole. A fella named Chip used to be there. Yeah, he did. Now, you heard of him. His name was Lewis Mathis. He was one of his kid over at trumpet players way back years ago and called him Chip. Well, I was in the Army and I used to go on watching him. I had my music up there but…
He's daddy, huh? Which, no, which Willie Humphrey? I mean there's a- The old man. Not Willie Humphrey would play the clarinet.

items.title: Ernest 'Punch' Miller Interview, 1960-04-04
items.q: when I was in the army, a fellow named Lewis Mathis called him Chiff. He tried to get me away from that, but I, you know, wouldn't listen to him until I got back yet.

ctx.x: Well, I play it like this now. And that's the standard. Yeah. Now who plays around inside of the lip way today? I see somebody doing that not long ago.

Some of the trumpet players. I forgot who it was though. Seems to me, Kit Howard plays that way now. I believe he does. Maybe Kit Clayton, I can't remember. One of them, yeah, one of them. But you can't get no power like that. You can't put nothing behind it. I wonder why people started that way. I did. I started wrong by not having nobody to share. Of course, when I was in the army, a fellow named Lewis Mathis called him Chiff. He tried to get me away from that, but I, you know, wouldn't listen to him until I…
Oh, oh, oh. What are some of the other different ways that guys had of lipping their horns?
